abstract: This study analyzes the spread and consumption of fake news on Twitter during the 2016 U.S. presidential election by linking Twitter accounts to registered voters. It measures who was exposed to fake news, who shared it, and how fake news related to consumption of factual news. The findings reveal that exposure to and sharing of fake news were highly concentrated among a small subset of users.
key_claims: Fake news exposure and sharing during the 2016 election were heavily concentrated among a small fraction of Twitter users rather than broadly distributed.
Fake news constituted a relatively small share of overall news consumption on the platform.
Linking social media accounts to voter records enables identification of who consumes and spreads fake news.
methods: Analysis of Twitter data during the 2016 U.S. presidential election cycle.
Matching Twitter accounts to specific registered voters to characterize exposure and sharing.
Quantifying fake news consumption relative to factual news consumption.
findings: Fake news accounted for nearly 6% of all news consumption.
Only 1% of users were exposed to 80% of fake news.
0.1% of users were responsible for sharing the majority of fake news (per abstract; exact figure truncated in source).
contributions: Provides empirical, individual-level evidence on the concentration of fake news exposure and dissemination.
Demonstrates a methodology of matching social media accounts to voter records for studying political information consumption.
framing: The paper contributes to research on misinformation and political communication in the digital age, situating itself within debates about the prevalence and impact of fake news during the 2016 election (accompanied by a Perspective commentary by Ruths).
